subject: Dedicated capacity: priority queue behavior & SLA exception request (Midwest Energy)
messages:
From: Tom Greene <t.greene@midwestenergy.com>
To: laura_bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
Cc: procurement@midwestenergy.com, Alicia Romero <alicia.romero@midwestenergy.com>
Date: Thu, 5 Mar 2026 09:12:43 -0500
Subject: Dedicated capacity SLA exception request

Hi Laura —

Thanks for the demo last week. As we work through procurement and internal risk approvals, our security and ops teams flagged two requirements that are blocking sign-off unless we can get them addressed in the Dedicated capacity contract: 

1) Uptime: We need a written exception guaranteeing 99.95% availability for the reserved pool (8 GPUs) across our primary region during business hours (M–F 6:00–20:00 CT).
2) Latency / queueing: For our high-priority inference path (inference size ~4k tokens, batch size 1), we need assurance that queueing will not introduce more than 50ms P95 added latency, and that a burst to 12 GPUs (for up to 30 minutes) can be accommodated without request queuing beyond 200 requests.

We attached a short checklist and a requested capacity sheet to illustrate the workload. I realize some of this is non-standard — happy to discuss trade-offs. Procurement would like a proposed exception letter and a simple credit schedule if thresholds aren’t met.

Can you confirm feasibility and next steps? We’re trying to close the contract by the end of March.

Thanks,
Tom Greene
Head of Cloud Ops — Midwest Energy
Attachment: Midwest_Energy_SLA_Checklist.pdf (pdf), requested_capacity_sheet.xlsx (xlsx)

Tom —

Thanks for the clear ask and the attachments, I’ve reviewed the checklist. Short answer: some of this we can cover with a combination of reserved capacity guarantees and operational controls, but a hard promise on absolute queueing latency requires engineering agreement on the exact definition and measurable SLOs. I’ve looped in Vivek (runtime/infra) and Neha (sales/procurement lead) so we can scope the commitment and a credit schedule.

Two quick clarifying questions to help us scope:
- Is the 99.95% requirement intended to be 24x7 or only for the business-hours window you specified?
- For the 50ms P95 queueing add: is that the total added queueing (server-side only) or the end-to-end p95 you want us to guarantee?

Tentative next steps from our side:
1) Engineering to comment on feasibility and measurable SLOs (Vivek).
2) Sales/procurement to draft an exception letter and credit schedule once we have measurable SLOs (Neha + me).
3) If needed, we’ll propose mitigations: pre-warmed pools, priority queueing for high-priority tokens, and a defined burst capacity window.

Can you confirm the answers to the two bullets above? I’ll aim to get an internal technical read by EOD 3/6.

Best,
Laura Bennett

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity SLA exception request — technical read

Laura / Neha / Ben —

Technical read (high-level):

Summary: We can meet the spirit of Midwest Energy’s ask with a combination of reserved GPU capacity, priority queues, and explicit bursting rules. However, we should avoid promising an absolute fixed microsecond/millisecond queueing guarantee; instead we provide measurable SLOs with clear operational controls and an agreed mitigation policy.

Details:
- Reserved pool: We can reserve an 8-GPU pool pinned for ME during the business-hours window. Reservation reduces noisy neighbor risk and ensures dedicated lanes for preemptible work.
- Burst to 12 GPUs: We can implement a short burst window (configurable up to 30 minutes) that allows autoscaling from 8 -> 12 GPUs if capacity is available in the region. Burst is not instantaneous — it requires node provisioning and KV cache warmup; recommend we define a pre-warm run (fast path) to reduce coldstart to ~60–90s.
- Queueing behavior: Server-side queueing can be controlled with priority queues: high-priority requests go to a reserved execution queue with headroom. We can guarantee a P95 server-side queueing addition no worse than X ms under normal conditions; I suggest we define X as 75ms for the signed exception (we can try to improve to 50ms after an initial 30-day run-in). The reason we avoid 50ms as a hard guarantee today is kernel warmups and GPU context rehydration under some model configs (4k tokens) can add jitter.
- Latency SLO: We can commit to a latency SLO for the high-priority path (P95 generation time excluding network) and measure with our tracing (we’ll surface token-level breakdowns in the Console).
- Credits & escalation: If we miss the agreed availability SLO (proposed 99.95% for business-hours) or the latency SLO for the high-priority path, we recommend a tiered credit schedule: 10% credit for first breach window, 25% for repeated breaches within a 30-day period.

Operational recommendations:
1) Pre-warm job before expected heavy windows (we can provide an API to trigger pre-warm).
2) Use priority headers in requests to ensure correct routing into the reserved queue.
3) Monthly runbook sync between Redwood SRE and ME ops for capacity planning.

Open items for contract language:
- Finalize measurable definition of "server-side queueing add" (exact measurement points).
- Agree on burst availability SLAs (we can commit to offering burst but guarantee limited contractual penalties tied to provisioning time).

I attached an excerpt from our Dedicated runbook that describes pre-warm and priority queue behavior. Happy to talk through on a call — I can be available 3/9 10–11 CT.

– Vivek
VP, Infrastructure — Redwood Inference
Attachment: redwood_dedicated_runbook_excerpt.txt

Date: Mon, 8 Mar 2026 16:20:02 -05:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity SLA exception request

Tom / Alicia —

Thanks for the patience while we scoped this internally. Summary of what Redwood can offer for the Dedicated pool (proposal):

- Availability: Contracted exception for business-hours availability (M–F 06:00–20:00 CT) with a target uptime of 99.95% for the reserved 8-GPU pool. Credits: 10% usage credit for a single incident window below threshold, 25% for repeated breaches within 30 days.
- Burst: Support for a configurable burst window up to 30 minutes enabling scaling from 8 -> 12 GPUs when capacity exists in-region. We will commit to proactive capacity planning and provide a pre-warm API; however, we cannot guarantee instantaneous provisioning.
- Queueing / latency: We propose an initial contractual P95 server-side queueing addition of 75ms for the high-priority inference path (4k token requests), with a 30-day run-in period to try to hit 50ms. End-to-end latency guarantees (including network) are not included. We will instrument token-level tracing and share dashboards for verification.
- Operational controls: Priority headers, pre-warm API, monthly ops sync, and an SRE escalation path.

Next steps:
1) Neha will send a draft exception letter and credit schedule reflecting the bullets above (today EOD).
2) If the terms look acceptable, we’ll send a DocuSign packet for signature and schedule a runbook alignment call (suggest 3/12).
3) Vivek’s team will prepare the pre-warm playbook and a short verification checklist for ME ops.

Tom — can you confirm you have internal approval to proceed on this basis and whether procurement needs any additional artifacts (PO templates, vendor compliance docs)? Once you confirm, Neha will circulate the paperwork.

Best regards,
Laura Bennett
Director, Strategic Accounts — Redwood Inference
